claim: TRPV4 is the temperature-sensitive ion channel of human sperm
source: TRPV4 is the temperature-sensitive ion channel of human sperm
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including electrophysiology, pharmacology, and molecular biology

claim: Ion channels control the ability of human sperm to fertilize the egg by triggering hyperactivated motility
source: Ion channels control the ability of human sperm to fertilize the egg by triggering hyperactivated motility, which is regulated by membrane potential, intracellular pH, and cytosolic calcium.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge

claim: Three essential ion channels regulate sperm hyperactivation: CatSper (Ca2+ channel), KSper (K+ channel), and Hv1 (H+ channel)
source: Previous studies unraveled three essential ion channels that regulate these parameters: (1) the Ca2+ channel CatSper, (2) the K+ channel KSper, and (3) the H+ channel Hv1.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous research findings

claim: The molecular identity of the sperm Na+ conductance that mediates initial membrane depolarization has not been defined prior to this study
source: However, the molecular identity of the sperm Na+ conductance that mediates initial membrane depolarization and, thus, triggers downstream signaling events is yet to be defined.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses

claim: DSper is functionally expressed at both mRNA and protein levels in human sperm
source: It is functionally expressed at both mRNA and protein levels, while other temperature-sensitive TRPV channels are not functional in human sperm.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR, Western blotting, and immunocytochemistry data presented in the manuscript

claim: Other temperature-sensitive TRPV channels are not functional in human sperm
source: It is functionally expressed at both mRNA and protein levels, while other temperature-sensitive TRPV channels are not functional in human sperm.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological testing with agonists for TRPV1, TRPV3, and TRPM3 showing no effects

claim: DSper currents are activated by warm temperatures
source: DSper currents are activated by warm temperatures and mediate cation conductance, that shares a pharmacological profile reminiscent of TRPV4.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings showing current potentiation with temperature increases from 22°C to 37°C

claim: DSper mediates cation conductance with a pharmacological profile reminiscent of TRPV4
source: DSper currents are activated by warm temperatures and mediate cation conductance, that shares a pharmacological profile reminiscent of TRPV4.
evidence: This is supported by responses to TRPV4-specific agonists and antagonists

claim: TRPV4 activation triggers initial membrane depolarization, facilitating both CatSper and Hv1 gating and sperm hyperactivation
source: Together, these results suggest that TRPV4 activation triggers initial membrane depolarization, facilitating both CatSper and Hv1 gating and, consequently, sperm hyperactivation.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanistic model based on the experimental findings

claim: Human spermatozoa must sense the environment and adapt their motility to navigate the female reproductive tract and fertilize the egg
source: The ability of human spermatozoa to navigate the female reproductive tract and eventually locate and fertilize the egg is essential for reproduction (Okabe, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation

claim: Sperm motility is controlled in part by ATP production and flagellar ion homeostasis
source: To accomplish these goals, a spermatozoon must sense the environment and adapt its motility, which is controlled in part by ATP production and flagellar ion homeostasis (Lishko et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work

claim: Hyperactivated motility is an asymmetrical, high-amplitude, whip-like beating pattern of the flagellum that enables sperm to overcome the egg's protective vestments
source: Of vital importance is the transition from symmetrical basal tail bending into 'hyperactivated motility' – an asymmetrical, high-amplitude, whip-like beating pattern of the flagellum - that enables sperm to overcome the egg's protective vestments (Ho et al., 2002; Ishijima et al., 2006; Quill et al., 2003; Suarez, 1996, 2008, 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations

claim: Progesterone acts as a major trigger of human sperm hyperactivation
source: The steroid hormone progesterone (P4) acts as a major trigger of human sperm hyperactivation (Suarez, 2008; Uhler et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous research

claim: Progesterone is released by cumulus cells surrounding the egg
source: P4 is released by cumulus cells surrounding the egg (Schuetz and Dubin, 1981) and causes a robust elevation of human sperm cytoplasmic [Ca2+] via the principal Ca2+ channel of sperm, CatSper (EC50 = 7.7 ± 1.8 nM) (Lishko et al., 2011; Strünker et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: Progesterone causes a robust elevation of human sperm cytoplasmic Ca2+ via CatSper with EC50 = 7.7 ± 1.8 nM
source: P4 is released by cumulus cells surrounding the egg (Schuetz and Dubin, 1981) and causes a robust elevation of human sperm cytoplasmic [Ca2+] via the principal Ca2+ channel of sperm, CatSper (EC50 = 7.7 ± 1.8 nM) (Lishko et al., 2011; Strünker et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous research

claim: Progesterone acts via its non-genomic receptor ABHD2, a serine hydrolase that releases inhibition of human CatSper upon P4 binding
source: The steroid acts via its non-genomic receptor ABHD2, a serine hydrolase that, upon P4 binding, releases inhibition of human CatSper (Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work

claim: Ca2+ influx through CatSper channels is necessary for fertilization and initiates hyperactivated motility
source: The Ca2+ influx produced from the opening of CatSper channels is a necessary milestone in the process of fertilization and initiates hyperactivated motility (Suarez, 2008; Carlson et al., 2005, 2003; Chung et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2007; Navarro et al., 2008; Qi et al., 2007; Quill et al., 2003; Ren et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations

claim: Human CatSper exhibits weak voltage-dependency with half-maximal activation at V1/2 = +70 mV for capacitated sperm cells
source: CatSper channels exhibit weak voltage-dependency with half-maximal activation at V1/2 human CatSper =+70 mV for capacitated sperm cells (Lishko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work

claim: Only a small fraction of human CatSper channels are open at physiological-relevant membrane potentials
source: Given this unusually high V1/2, only a small fraction of human CatSper channels are open at physiological-relevant membrane potentials.
evidence: This is inferred from the V1/2 value of +70 mV

claim: Progesterone potentiates CatSper activity by shifting V1/2 to more negative values (V1/2 = +30 mV with 500 nM P4)
source: P4 has been shown to potentiate CatSper activity by shifting V1/2 to more negative values (V1/2 human CatSper =+30 mV with 500 nM P4 for capacitated sperm cells [Lishko et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: CatSper requires both intracellular alkalization and significant membrane depolarization to function properly
source: However, CatSper still requires both additional intracellular alkalization and significant membrane depolarization to function properly (Lishko et al., 2011; Kirichok et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations

claim: Hv1 is a potential regulator of intracellular pH in human spermatozoa
source: The proton channel Hv1 was revealed as one of the potential regulators of intracellular pH (pHi) in human spermatozoa (Lishko et al., 2010; Berger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations

claim: Hv1 mediates unidirectional flow of protons to the extracellular environment
source: By mediating unidirectional flow of protons to the extracellular environment, Hv1 represents an important component in the CatSper activation cascade, but it also induces membrane hyperpolarization by exporting positive charges out of the cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: Hv1 induces membrane hyperpolarization by exporting positive charges out of the cell
source: By mediating unidirectional flow of protons to the extracellular environment, Hv1 represents an important component in the CatSper activation cascade, but it also induces membrane hyperpolarization by exporting positive charges out of the cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: Hv1 is a voltage-gated channel that depends on membrane depolarization to be activated
source: Hv1 is a voltage-gated channel and depends on membrane depolarization to be activated (Ramsey et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations

claim: Both CatSper and Hv1 must rely on yet unidentified depolarizing ion channels
source: Therefore, both CatSper and Hv1 must rely on yet unidentified depolarizing ion channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the voltage-dependence of both channels

claim: Progesterone inhibits the K+ channel KSper with IC50 = 7.5 ± 1.3 μM
source: P4 was shown to inhibit the K+ channel of human sperm KSper (IC50 = 7.5 ± 1.3 μM [Mannowetz et al., 2013; Brenker et al., 2014]) making KSper inhibition one of the potential origins for membrane depolarization.
evidence: This is stated with citations

claim: Efficient KSper inhibition requires P4 concentrations in the μM range, which are only present in close vicinity of the egg
source: However, efficient KSper inhibition requires P4 concentrations in the μM range, which are only present in close vicinity of the egg.
evidence: This is inferred from the IC50 value and physiological P4 concentrations

claim: Sperm hyperactivation occurs in the fallopian tubes, where P4 concentrations are not sufficient to block KSper
source: Sperm hyperactivation, however, occurs in the fallopian tubes, where P4 concentrations are not sufficient to block KSper (Demott and Suarez, 1992).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: The current model is missing a fourth member – the 'Depolarizing Channel of Sperm' (DSper)
source: Hence, the current model is missing a fourth member – the 'Depolarizing Channel of Sperm' (DSper) (Miller et al., 2015).
evidence: This establishes the hypothesis that the study tests

claim: Activation of DSper would induce long-lasting membrane depolarization and provide the necessary positive net charge influx for CatSper/Hv1 activity
source: Activation of the hypothetical DSper ion channel would induce long-lasting membrane depolarization and provide the necessary positive net charge influx for CatSper/Hv1 activity.
evidence: This is the proposed function of DSper based on the requirements of CatSper and Hv1

claim: CatSper conducts monovalent ions such as Cs+ and Na+ in the absence of divalent cations
source: As many calcium channels, CatSper conducts monovalent ions, such as Cs+ and Na+ in the absence of divalent cations from the extracellular solution (divalent free; DVF) (Lishko et al., 2011; Kirichok et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations

claim: CatSper is permeable to Ca2+ and Ba2+, but cannot conduct Mg2+
source: CatSper is also permeable to Ca2+ and Ba2+, but it cannot conduct Mg2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—source data 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Extracellular Mg2+ blocks the CatSper pore, resulting in inhibition of monovalent CatSper currents
source: In the presence of extracellular Mg2+ the CatSper pore is blocked, resulting in the inhibition of monovalent CatSper currents (ICatSper) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—source data 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Residual currents remain when ICatSper is blocked with 1 mM extracellular Mg2+
source: In whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings from human ejaculated spermatozoa, we consistently observed residual currents when ICatSper was blocked with 1 mM extracellular Mg2+ (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiological recordings in Figure 1A,B

claim: Cs+ inward and outward currents under DVF condition are larger than currents recorded in the presence of Mg2+
source: Cs+ inward and outward currents elicited under DVF condition (black traces and bars) were larger than currents recorded in the presence of Mg2+ (red traces and bars) (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—source data 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A-C

claim: The residual conductance in the presence of Mg2+ is observed in both noncapacitated and capacitated spermatozoa
source: This phenomenon was observed in both noncapacitated and capacitated spermatozoa, respectively.
evidence: This is stated based on the experimental observations

claim: Capacitated cells show increased current densities under both DVF and Mg2+ conditions
source: Notably, capacitated cells generally showed increased current densities under both conditions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C

claim: The remaining conductance after Mg2+ block is a novel non-CatSper conductance via DSper
source: The data suggests that the remaining conductance is a novel non-CatSper conductance via the yet to be identified DSper ion channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing residual currents after CatSper block

claim: DSper currents are potentiated during capacitation
source: DSper currents were potentiated during capacitation (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1A) and exhibited outward rectification, though, DSper currents recorded from capacitated cells were notably less rectifying (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1A,B

claim: DSper currents exhibit outward rectification
source: DSper currents were potentiated during capacitation (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1A) and exhibited outward rectification, though, DSper currents recorded from capacitated cells were notably less rectifying (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: DSper currents from capacitated cells are less rectifying than from noncapacitated cells
source: DSper currents were potentiated during capacitation (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1A) and exhibited outward rectification, though, DSper currents recorded from capacitated cells were notably less rectifying (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is observed in the current traces in Figure 1A,B

claim: 1 mM Mg2+ is sufficient to completely block ICatSper and selectively isolate DSper currents
source: To rule out 'contamination' of putative IDSper with remaining ICatSper, we next tested whether 1 mM Mg2+ is sufficient to completely block ICatSper and selectively isolate DSper currents.
evidence: This is tested experimentally with the CatSper inhibitor NNC 55-0396

claim: The CatSper inhibitor NNC 55-0396 does not elicit any additional inhibitory effect on IDSper
source: The CatSper inhibitor NNC 55–0396 (Lishko et al., 2011; Strünker et al., 2011) did not elicit any additional inhibitory effect on IDSper (Figure 1D–F; Figure 1—source data 1A), confirming efficient CatSper pore block by Mg2+.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D-F

claim: A novel CatSper-independent cation conductance could provide additional depolarization under physiological conditions
source: These findings corroborate our hypothesis that a novel CatSper-independent cation conductance could provide additional depolarization under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings

claim: Elevating temperature profoundly increases IDSper
source: As shown in Figure 2A–C, elevating temperature profoundly increased IDSper.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-C

claim: Temperature-induced potentiation of DSper currents is observed in both noncapacitated and capacitated human spermatozoa
source: We observed a temperature-induced potentiation of both inward and outward currents in noncapacitated, as well as capacitated human spermatozoa (Figure 2A–B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A-B

claim: A temperature ramp from 23°C to 37°C potentiates IDSper inward currents by factors of 2.7 ± 0.5 for noncapacitated cells and 2.0 ± 0.2 for capacitated cells
source: A temperature ramp from 23°C to 37°C potentiated IDSper inward currents by factors of 2.7 ± 0.5 for noncapacitated cells and 2.0 ± 0.2 for capacitated cells, respectively (Q10 noncapacitated=1.76, Q10 capacitated=1.65 for caesium inward currents).
evidence: This is quantified from the experimental data

claim: Q10 for caesium inward currents is 1.76 for noncapacitated cells and 1.65 for capacitated cells
source: A temperature ramp from 23°C to 37°C potentiated IDSper inward currents by factors of 2.7 ± 0.5 for noncapacitated cells and 2.0 ± 0.2 for capacitated cells, respectively (Q10 noncapacitated=1.76, Q10 capacitated=1.65 for caesium inward currents).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data

claim: Half-maximal activation of DSper is achieved at T1/2 = 34°C for noncapacitated cells and T1/2 = 31°C for capacitated cells
source: Half-maximal activation was achieved at T1/2 = 34°C (noncapacitated) and T1/2 = 31°C (capacitated) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D

claim: The temperature-induced potentiation effect is reversible for both noncapacitated and capacitated cells
source: Moreover, the temperature-induced potentiation effect was reversible for both noncapacitated and capacitated cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E

claim: DSper is temperature-activated
source: We hence concluded that the observed phenomenon is not a temperature-induced loss of the seal and compromised membrane stability and that DSper is indeed temperature-activated.
evidence: This is concluded from the reversibility of the temperature effect

claim: Sodium is the major extracellular ion in the female reproductive tract at concentrations of 140-150 mM
source: Since sodium (Na+) is the major extracellular ion in the female reproductive tract ([Na+]=140–150 mM [Borland et al., 1980]), Na+ is a likely source for membrane depolarization.
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: DSper conducts Na+ with similar outward rectifying currents as observed with Cs+
source: As indicated in Figure 3A, similar outward rectifying DSper currentswere recorded when extracellular Cs+ was replaced with equimolar concentrations of Na+.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A

claim: DSper inward Na+ currents are entirely CatSper-independent
source: DSper inward Na+ currents were entirely CatSper-independent, since NNC 55–0396 had no significant inhibitory effect (Figure 3B,C; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: IDSper with Na+ is reversibly activated by warm temperatures in the presence of both 1 mM Mg2+ and 1 μM NNC 55-0396
source: In the presence of both 1 mM Mg2+ and 1 μM NNC 55–0396, IDSper was still reversibly activated by warm temperatures (Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—source data 1) with a 4.1 ± 0.5 fold increase for the inward sodium currents from 22°C to 37°C, which is notably larger than the fold-increase as observed for cesium currents (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D,E

claim: Temperature activation of DSper Na+ currents shows a 4.1 ± 0.5 fold increase from 22°C to 37°C
source: In the presence of both 1 mM Mg2+ and 1 μM NNC 55–0396, IDSper was still reversibly activated by warm temperatures (Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—source data 1) with a 4.1 ± 0.5 fold increase for the inward sodium currents from 22°C to 37°C, which is notably larger than the fold-increase as observed for cesium currents (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is quantified from the experimental data

claim: Half-maximum activation of DSper Na+ currents is at T1/2 = 34°C
source: Half -maximum activation was at T1/2 = 34°C, comparable to previously analyzed values for the temperature-activated Cs+ currents, however sodium conductance via DSper produced a larger Q10 noncapacitated=2.30.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data

claim: Q10 for sodium conductance via DSper is 2.30 for noncapacitated cells
source: Half -maximum activation was at T1/2 = 34°C, comparable to previously analyzed values for the temperature-activated Cs+ currents, however sodium conductance via DSper produced a larger Q10 noncapacitated=2.30.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data

claim: DSper shares characteristic hallmarks with thermosensitive TRPV channels
source: Together, these electrophysiological data indicate that DSper shares characteristic hallmarks with thermosensitive TRPV channels (Benham et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the temperature sensitivity and other properties

claim: Based on the IDSper temperature spectrum, candidate channels could be TRPV3, TRPM3 or TRPV4
source: Based on the observed IDSper temperature spectrum (Figures 2D and 3E), candidate channels could be TRPV3, TRPM3 or TRPV4 (Benham et al., 2003; Güler et al., 2002; Watanabe et al., 2002; Cheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the temperature activation range and cited literature

claim: TRPV2 is ruled out as a candidate because it has an unusually steep activation threshold above 53°C
source: We have ruled out TRPV2 involvement, since TRPV2 has an unusually steep activation threshold of above 53°C (Moore and Liedtke, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: TRPV1 was previously proposed as a mediator of human sperm thermotaxis
source: In addition, TRPV1 was previously proposed as a mediator of human sperm thermotaxis (De Toni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: Only TRPV4 agonist RN1747 elicited a significant effect among the tested TRP channel agonists
source: Employing either electrophysiological, or Ca2+ imaging recordings, only TRPV4 agonist RN1747 elicited a significant effect.
evidence: This is based on testing multiple agonists

claim: Application of 10 μM RN1747 significantly potentiates DSper outward currents in noncapacitated human sperm
source: In detail, application of 10 μM RN1747 (EC50 = 0.77 μM [Vincent et al., 2009]) significantly potentiated DSper outward currents (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—source data 1A) in noncapacitated human sperm.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: Capsaicin at 1 μM or 10 μM has no effect on DSper currents
source: In contrast, no effects were observed by 1 μM or 10 μM capsaicin (EC50 = 711.9 nM [Caterina et al., 1997]) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 1B-D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Addition of 30 µM PI4,5P2 to the pipette solution does not generate capsaicin-induced potentiation of DSper activity
source: In order to confirm TRPV1 functional absence, we repeated these capsaicin experiments with 30 µM PI4,5P2 inside, to account for a possible loss of capsaicin sensitivity due to potential depletion of endogenous PI4,5P2 during whole-cell recording (Bevan et al., 2014; Senning et al., 2014). However, no change in DSper inward- and outward currents was observed.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental results

claim: 10 μM capsaicin has no effect on cytosolic calcium levels in human sperm
source: Using Ca2+ imaging of fluo-4/AM-loaded sperm, we next recorded fluorescence changes in the flagellar principle piece while stimulating human sperm with either 10 μM capsaicin or 500 μM carvacrol (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—source data 1C,D). Neither TRPV1 nor TRPV3 agonist elicited any rise in cytosolic calcium levels.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: 500 μM carvacrol has no effect on cytosolic calcium levels in human sperm
source: Using Ca2+ imaging of fluo-4/AM-loaded sperm, we next recorded fluorescence changes in the flagellar principle piece while stimulating human sperm with either 10 μM capsaicin or 500 μM carvacrol (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—source data 1C,D). Neither TRPV1 nor TRPV3 agonist elicited any rise in cytosolic calcium levels.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Human spermatozoa do not express functional TRPV1 or TRPV3 channels
source: We thus concluded that human spermatozoa do not express functional TRPV1 or TRPV3 channels.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of response to specific agonists

claim: Application of 10 µM pregnenolone sulfate does not result in any change of the basal DSper current
source: Therefore, we have tested the possibility of TRPM3 involvement in IDSper generation by applying the TRPM3 agonist pregnenolone sulfate (PS) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Figure 4—source data 1E). Application of 10 µM PS did not result in any change of the basal DSper current, confirming the absence of functional TRPM3 in human spermatozoa.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Human spermatozoa do not express functional TRPM3
source: Application of 10 µM PS did not result in any change of the basal DSper current, confirming the absence of functional TRPM3 in human spermatozoa.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of response to pregnenolone sulfate

claim: The temperature-activated cation channel TRPV4 is likely functionally expressed and provides membrane depolarization in human sperm
source: Taking together, our results indicate that the temperature-activated cation channel TRPV4 is likely to be functionally expressed and provides membrane depolarization in human sperm.
evidence: This is concluded from the pharmacological and electrophysiological data

claim: Both TRPV4-specific antagonists HC067047 and RN1734 prevent temperature activation of DSper
source: Interestingly, additional pharmacological investigation of DSper revealed that both TRPV4-specific antagonists, HC067047 and RN1734 (Vincent et al., 2009; Everaerts et al., 2010), prevented temperature activation of DSper, confirming that DSper pharmacology matches that of TRPV4 (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A-C

claim: 0.1% ethanol vehicle control does not inhibit DSper temperature activation
source: Since both inhibitors are dissolved in ethanol, we performed a vehicle control to exclude any inhibitory effect of ethanol on temperature activation. Indeed, the same vehicle concentration (0.1% ethanol) failed to inhibit DSper temperature activation and yielded results comparable to the control conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—source data 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: TRPV4 was detected in human sperm on both mRNA and protein levels
source: Supporting our functional data, TRPV4 was detected in human sperm on both mRNA and protein levels.
evidence: This is stated based on RT-PCR and Western blotting results

claim: RT-PCR with mRNA from swim-up purified spermatozoa produced a band of expected size for full-length TRPV4
source: Reverse transcriptase PCR performed with mRNA isolated from "swim-up" purified spermatozoa, followed by an amplification of the full-length TRPV4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), produced a band of the expected size.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: The RT-PCR band was absent in negative controls without reverse transcriptase and without template
source: The band was absent in negative controls, to which no reverse transcriptase and no templates were added.
evidence: This is stated based on the RT-PCR results

claim: The sequence of the isolated PCR product yielded the full-length sequence of TRPV4 isoform A (2620 bp, 98 kDa)
source: The sequence of the isolated PCR product of that specific band (dotted square), yielded the full-length sequence of TRPV4 isoform A (2620 bp, 98 kDa, Q9ERZ8).
evidence: This is stated based on sequencing results

claim: TRPV4 protein was detected at ~115 kDa in extracts from human testicular tissue, capacitated and noncapacitated spermatozoa
source: Moreover, the presence of TRPV4 protein was confirmed by western blotting (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B). Immunoreactive bands were detected at ~115 kDa in extracts from human testicular tissue (1), capacitated (2) and noncapacitated (3) spermatozoa (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: Immunostaining with anti-hTRPV4 antibodies yielded an immunopositive signal in the acrosome and flagellum
source: Immunostaining with anti-hTRPV4 specific antibodies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C) yielded an immunopositive signal in the acrosome and flagellum.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: TRPV4 cloned from human sperm mRNA and expressed in HEK293 cells produces a band of similar molecular weight to sperm TRPV4
source: Finally, when TRPV4 was cloned from human sperm mRNA extracts and recombinantly expressed in HEK293 cells (Figure 6A), a band of similar molecular weight could be detected by western blotting (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B

claim: TRPV4 cloned from human sperm recapitulates DSper temperature sensitivity
source: Moreover, TRPV4 cloned from human sperm mRNA recapitulates DSper temperature sensitivity (Figure 6D–E; Figure 6—source data 1), as well as activation by the selective TRPV4 agonist RN1747 (Figure 6F–G; Figure 6—source data 1), indicating that TRPV4 cloned from human sperm cells indeed assembles into a functional channel.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D-E

claim: TRPV4 cloned from human sperm is activated by the selective TRPV4 agonist RN1747
source: Moreover, TRPV4 cloned from human sperm mRNA recapitulates DSper temperature sensitivity (Figure 6D–E; Figure 6—source data 1), as well as activation by the selective TRPV4 agonist RN1747 (Figure 6F–G; Figure 6—source data 1), indicating that TRPV4 cloned from human sperm cells indeed assembles into a functional channel.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F-G

claim: Sperm transition to hyperactivated motility is essential for fertilization
source: Sperm transition to hyperactivated motility is essential for fertilization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: Hyperactivation provides the propulsion force required to penetrate through viscous luminal fluids and protective vestments of the egg
source: Hyperactivation provides the propulsion force required to penetrate through viscous luminal fluids of the female reproductive tract and protective vestments of the egg.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: CatSper is a key player in the transition to hyperactivated motility
source: The CatSper channel is a key player in the transition to hyperactivated motility (Ren et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: Proper CatSper function requires three concurrent activation mechanisms: membrane depolarization, intracellular alkalization, and abundance of progesterone
source: However, proper CatSper function requires three concurrent activation mechanisms: (1) membrane depolarization (Lishko et al., 2011; Kirichok et al., 2006), (2) intracellular alkalization (Lishko et al., 2011; Kirichok et al., 2006), and for primate CatSper specifically (3) abundance of progesterone (Lishko et al., 2011; Strünker et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013; Sumigama et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations

claim: The source of membrane depolarization in human sperm remained puzzling prior to this study
source: While the two latter mechanisms have been described in detail, the source of membrane depolarization remained puzzling.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap

claim: K+, Ca2+, Cl–, and H+ conductances have been described in human spermatozoa
source: In human spermatozoa, K+, Ca2+, Cl–, and H+ conductances have been described (Lishko et al., 2011; Strünker et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013; Lishko et al., 2010; Berger et al., 2017; Mannowetz et al., 2013; Brenker et al., 2014; Brown et al., 2016; Geng et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2015; Orta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations

claim: The molecular nature of Na+ conductance of sperm remained unknown prior to this study
source: However, the molecular nature of Na+ conductance of sperm remained unknown.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap

claim: Upon ejaculation, mammalian spermatozoa are exposed to increased Na+ concentration (~30 mM in cauda epididymis versus 100-150 mM in seminal plasma)
source: Upon ejaculation, mammalian spermatozoa are exposed to increased [Na+] (~30 mM in cauda epididymis versus 100–150 mM in seminal plasma).
evidence: This is stated as physiological fact

claim: In the female reproductive tract, Na+ levels are similar to those in serum (140-150 mM)
source: In the female reproductive tract, Na+ levels are similar to those in serum (140–150 mM) (Borland et al., 1980).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: Na+ is ideally suited to provide a depolarizing charge upon sperm deposit into the female reproductive tract
source: Hence, Na+ is ideally suited to provide a depolarizing charge upon sperm deposit into the female reproductive tract.
evidence: This is inferred from the Na+ concentration gradient

claim: A novel CatSper-independent cation conductance exhibits outward rectification and potentiation upon capacitation
source: Here, we recorded a novel CatSper-independent cation conductance that exhibits outward rectification as well as potentiation upon capacitation.
evidence: This is based on the electrophysiological recordings

claim: This novel conductance is carried by the hypothetical 'Depolarizing Channel of Sperm' DSper
source: We propose that this novel conductance is carried by the hypothetical 'Depolarizing Channel of Sperm' DSper and provides the necessary cation influx that ensures membrane depolarization.
evidence: This is the proposed interpretation of the data

claim: IDSper is activated by warm temperatures between 22 and 37°C
source: IDSper is activated by warm temperatures between 22 and 37°C (Figures 2 and 3D–E) which makes the protein thermoresponsive within the physiologically relevant temperatures (34.4°C in the epididymis (Valeri et al., 1993), 37°C body core temperature at the site of fertilization).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data in Figures 2 and 3

claim: The temperature range of DSper activation is physiologically relevant (34.4°C in the epididymis, 37°C at the site of fertilization)
source: IDSper is activated by warm temperatures between 22 and 37°C (Figures 2 and 3D–E) which makes the protein thermoresponsive within the physiologically relevant temperatures (34.4°C in the epididymis (Valeri et al., 1993), 37°C body core temperature at the site of fertilization).
evidence: This is stated with citation for epididymal temperature

claim: Capacitated rabbit and human sperm cells have an inherent temperature sensing ability
source: Previous studies showed that capacitated rabbit and human sperm cells have an inherent temperature sensing ability (Bahat et al., 2003), which could be an additional driving force to guide male gametes from the reservoir in the Fallopian tubes towards the warmer fertilization site.
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: Human spermatozoa likely express a temperature-activated ion channel that operates in the 22-37°C range and enables thermotaxis
source: It is thus very likely, that human spermatozoa express a temperature-activated ion channel, which operates in the described temperature range and enables thermotaxis.
evidence: This is inferred from the temperature sensing ability and the experimental findings

claim: The temperature-sensitive channel could serve as a sensor for the initiation of human sperm capacitation
source: Another potential role for this channel is to serve as a sensor for the initiation of human sperm capacitation.
evidence: This is proposed as a potential function

claim: During maturation in the female reproductive tract, human sperm are exposed to elevated temperature, especially before and during ovulation
source: During maturation in the female reproductive tract, human sperm are exposed to elevated temperature, especially before and during ovulation, which is correlated with an increase in basal body temperature by 1°C.
evidence: This is stated as physiological fact

claim: Ovulation is correlated with an increase in basal body temperature by 1°C
source: During maturation in the female reproductive tract, human sperm are exposed to elevated temperature, especially before and during ovulation, which is correlated with an increase in basal body temperature by 1°C.
evidence: This is stated as physiological fact

claim: Spermatozoa can survive in the female reproductive tract for several days by binding to the ciliated epithelia of the fallopian tubes
source: As spermatozoa are able to survive in the female reproductive tract for several days by binding to the ciliated epithelia of the fallopian tubes, they must eventually undergo hyperactivation to detach (Ardon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: Spermatozoa must undergo hyperactivation to detach from the fallopian tube epithelia
source: As spermatozoa are able to survive in the female reproductive tract for several days by binding to the ciliated epithelia of the fallopian tubes, they must eventually undergo hyperactivation to detach (Ardon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: CatSper-deficient spermatozoa that cannot hyperactivate are not able to ascend the fallopian tubes
source: Accordingly, CatSper-deficient spermatozoa that cannot hyperactivate are not able to ascend the fallopian tubes (Ho et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: Sperm capacitation takes approximately 5 hours in humans
source: In order for hyperactivation to occur, spermatozoa must be fully capacitated – a process that takes approximately 5 hr in humans, and requires sperm exposure to bicarbonate, albumin, and elevated temperature.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: Sperm capacitation requires exposure to bicarbonate, albumin, and elevated temperature
source: In order for hyperactivation to occur, spermatozoa must be fully capacitated – a process that takes approximately 5 hr in humans, and requires sperm exposure to bicarbonate, albumin, and elevated temperature.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: Exposure to 37°C is an absolute requirement for sperm capacitation in vitro
source: While sperm capacitation can be achieved in vitro, exposure to 37°C is an absolute requirement.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: The temperature response profile of DSper conforms with previously reported temperature sensitivity of TRPV4
source: The temperature response profile of DSper conforms with previously reported temperature sensitivity of TRPV4 (Benham et al., 2003; Güler et al., 2002; Watanabe et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations

claim: The absence of significant inward current via TRPV4 in presence of both extracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+ results from competition for the channel pore between divalent and monovalent ions
source: It should be noted that the absence of a significant inward current via TRPV4 in presence of both extracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+, such as in HS solution (Figure 1A–B), results from competition for the channel pore between the divalent and monovalent ions.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation

claim: Extracellular Ca2+ inhibits TRPV4 monovalent conductance
source: It has been reported that extracellular Ca2+ inhibits TRPV4 monovalent conductance (Watanabe et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: The temperature coefficient Q10 for recombinantly expressed TRPV4 has been reported to be between 9 and 19
source: The temperature coefficient Q10 reflects the temperature dependence of the membrane current and has been reported to be between 9 and 19 for recombinantly expressed TRPV4 (Güler et al., 2002; Watanabe et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations

claim: Endogenously expressed TRPV4 channels from aorta endothelial cells exhibit less steep temperature dependence than recombinant TRPV4
source: However, endogenously expressed TRPV4 channels recorded from aorta endothelial cells (Watanabe et al., 2002) exhibit less steep temperature dependence, which resembles the Q10 of sperm TRPV4 (Q10 sodium = 2.30, noncapacitated sperm).
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: Different lipid environments or additional channel modifications may be responsible for differences in Q10 between recombinant and endogenous TRPV4
source: It is possible that different lipid environments or additional channel modifications are responsible for such differences.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible explanation

claim: Sperm cells may possess more than one type of temperature-regulated ion channel
source: It is also possible that sperm cells possess more than one type of temperature-regulated ion channel.

claim: The biphasic inhibition of DSper with TRPV4-selective antagonists does not result in complete current inhibition, particularly between 24 and 32°C
source: The biphasic inhibition of DSper with TRPV4-selective antagonists (Figure 5) does not result in complete current inhibition, particularly in the temperate range between 24 and 32°C.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 5

claim: The incomplete inhibition may suggest an additional, non-TRPV4 conductance
source: This may suggest an additional, non-TRPV4 conductance.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete inhibition

claim: The additional conductance could be temperature-dependent release of NNC inhibition on CatSper or other undiscovered temperature-sensitive ion channels
source: The molecular nature of such additional conductance(s) could be either temperature-dependent release of NNC inhibition on CatSper or perhaps the presence of other yet undiscovered temperature-sensitive ion channel(s).
evidence: This is proposed as possible explanations

claim: Murine TRPV4 regulates sperm thermotaxis according to one published report
source: Interestingly, according to one published report (Hamano et al., 2016), murine TRPV4 regulates sperm thermotaxis.
evidence: This is stated with citation

claim: TRPV4-deficient male mice are fertile
source: However, TRPV4-deficient male mice are fertile which may indicate either presence of an additional temperature sensor or a compensatory mechanism.

claim: The fertility of TRPV4-deficient mice may indicate presence of an additional temperature sensor or a compensatory mechanism

claim: TRPV4-mediated Na+ influx induces membrane depolarization, which activates both Hv1 and CatSper
source: According to our model (Figure 7), human spermatozoa are exposed to an increase in both temperature and [Na+] upon deposit to the female reproductive tract. TRPV4-mediated Na+ influx induces membrane depolarization, which in turn activates both Hv1 and CatSper.
evidence: This is the proposed model shown in Figure 7

claim: H+ efflux through Hv1 promotes intracellular alkalization and enhanced CatSper activation
source: H+ efflux through Hv1 promotes intracellular alkalization and thus enhanced CatSper activation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model

claim: Approaching the egg, sperm is exposed to P4 and anandamide (AEA), both secreted by cumulus cells
source: Approaching the egg, sperm is exposed to P4 and the endocannabinoid anandamide (AEA), both secreted by cumulus cells (El-Talatini et al., 2009; Hunter and Rodriguez-Martinez, 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations

claim: AEA activates Hv1
source: P4 binding to ABHD2 releases CatSper inhibition (Miller et al., 2016) while AEA was shown to activate Hv1 (Lishko et al., 2010).

claim: The opening of CatSper generates a Ca2+ influx along the flagellum that triggers hyperactivation

claim: P4 not only potentiates CatSper, it also inhibits KSper-mediated hyperpolarization
source: P4 not only potentiates CatSper, it also inhibits KSper-mediated hyperpolarization, which gives the CatSper activation cascade an additional impulse (Mannowetz et al., 2013).
